title: Gesu Daraz: Darshan at a Sufi Gate
hookLine: a Sufi's tomb in the Deccan, Muslim rites inside, and a gate that lets everyone in
carry: darshan at the gate; the rites stay theirs
tomorrow: a fakir lives in a mosque named for Krishna's city?
last: NEITHER HAS TO BECOME THE OTHER.

cards: Exam week. A lucky pen, a candle, a grandmother's blessing at the door. In Gulbarga, on the Deccan plateau, some families carry that worry through the gate of a shrine.
The air smells of rose petals. Someone lays a cloth over a tomb. A child who's nervous about a test stands holding flowers.
The man buried here is a Sufi, remembered by the name Gesu Daraz. The family at the gate isn't Muslim. Nobody stops them, and nobody asks them to be anything other than what they are.

teach.b: The shrine is a dargah: the tomb of a Sufi saint and the place that grows up around it. Sufis are Muslims who walk a path of drawing near to God, often through a chain of teachers.
The man here, Khwaja Banda Nawaz, is remembered as a Chishti, one of the Sufi orders, and his nickname has a story.
Gesu Daraz means long locks. It's told that as a young disciple in Delhi he helped carry his teacher's palanquin, his long hair caught in it, and he walked on without a word.
A student's devotion to his teacher: this week's theme, from across the gate. The prayers at the tomb are Muslim prayers, and the yearly urs is kept by the shrine's Muslim community.

And Hindus come through the gate, with flowers, a thread, a bow. What they bring has a Hindu shape: darshan, seeing a holy one and being seen, honoring holiness where a saint has lived. Nobody asks them to convert.

Nobody turns the tomb into a temple. Now the week: a student who bows, asks and serves; viveka's lamp; the teacher as god, and only the good; Kabir's bhakti, his many names, the Lord in the heart. And this gate.

how: At Sufi dargahs such as Khwaja Banda Nawaz's in Gulbarga, the rites at the tomb are Muslim and the urs is kept by the shrine's community, while visitors of other faiths, Hindus among them, come with flowers and prayers for blessing.

games.q: your aunt wants to tie a thread at a Sufi dargah before a surgery. your cousin worries she'll offend the keepers. what fits the history?
o: go as a guest: the rites stay Muslim, and her prayer can be her own.

games.why: At a dargah, Hindu visitors come with flowers and a thread; the rites stay Muslim, and neither side gives itself up.

practice: Count on your fingers the people outside your own tradition who have welcomed you somewhere: a home, a table, a doorway. One finger for each. Stay a breath with each face before you move to the next.
If you run out of fingers, good. If you only reach one, that one counts too.

wordCard.voice: Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, a Sufi's tomb in the Deccan: Muslim rites inside, Hindu visitors at the gate.

carryVoice: Something to keep: darshan at the gate, and the rites stay theirs. That's the week.
